title: Not to distress you
hookLine: We did not send the Qur'an to make you miserable (20:2)
carry: the stones were never the point

lines: WHAT THE QUR'AN IS NOT FOR.
cards: Some people carry their faith like a backpack full of stones. Every missed prayer is a stone. Every slip is a stone.
They're trying so hard that the thing meant to hold them up is wearing them down. If that's ever been you, or someone you love, Surah twenty has something to say first.
It opens with two Arabic letters, and then, in its very first sentence, tells the Prophet what the Qur'an is not for.

teach.h: TA. HA. THE MEANING IS DEBATED.
teach.b: The two letters are Ta and Ha. Like the other letters that open some surahs, their meaning is debated. Some read Ta-Ha as a name for the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and Taha is given as a boy's name for that reason.

Others said it means O man, in an old dialect. Others simply said: God knows best. Then verse two, in Pickthall's words: "We have not revealed unto thee (Muhammad) this Qur'an that thou shouldst be distressed".
The word is tashqa: to be wretched, worn out, miserable. It shares a root with the word Zakariyya used in Surah Maryam: I have never been left wretched in my prayer to You.
Two surahs in a row, the same root: a man never left wretched by prayer, and a Qur'an not sent to make anyone wretched. Commentators give reasons for the verse.
One report says the Prophet stood in night prayer so long his feet swelled. Another says his opponents mocked him: this Qur'an has made you miserable. The verse answers both.
Verse three says what the Qur'an is for: a reminder, for whoever stands in awe.
A hadith in Bukhari puts it plainly: the religion is ease, and nobody makes it hard on themselves except that it overcomes them. So aim for what's right, come close to it, and be of good cheer.
This doesn't mean faith asks nothing.
Ta-Ha goes on to tell Musa's long story, which is anything but easy. But it begins by saying what the weight is for. Not misery.

how: Muslim teachers cite 20:2, 2:185 and the hadith 'the religion is ease' to warn against making religion a burden; Taha is also used as a given name, from the opening letters of this surah.

sh-q-y: wretched, worn out. Zakariyya was never left so by prayer; the Qur'an wasn't sent to make the Prophet so.

it says the Qur'an isn't for misery, but a reminder; the surah goes on to tell Musa's hard road.

games.q: you've been praying so long at night that your feet are swelling, and people mock you that the Qur'an has made you miserable. what does 20:2 say?
o: pray even longer to prove them wrong.
We did not send the Qur'an down to you to distress you.
games.why: the Qur'an wasn't revealed to make him wretched, but as a reminder (20:2–3). commentators connect the verse to both reports.

practice: Notice if there's anything you carry about your faith, or about trying to be a good person, that feels like a stone: a guilt, a standard you never meet, a practice you dread.
Name it, and ask what it was meant to be for: remembering, rest, connection. If you pray, you can ask for ease in it; if not, just let the stone sit down beside you for a while.

wordCard.voice: Ta-Ha. The surah that opens by promising the Qur'an wasn't sent to wear anyone out, but as a reminder. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the letters ta and ha that open Surah 20; also a given name.
